resources.string: Oaks, beeches and chestnuts: dry fruits associated with a cupule.
Birches, alders, hornbeams and hazels: unisexual flowers, often in catkins, and dry fruits.
In this atlas: maples with opposite leaves and winged fruits, and horse chestnut with palmately compound leaves.
In this atlas: ash and privet, both with opposite leaves but very different fruits.
This family includes lindens: alternate leaves and a flower cluster associated with a long bract.
A diverse family: often five petals and many stamens; a wide range of fruit types.
In this atlas: aspen, with catkins and small hairy seeds.
Needle-bearing conifers with cones; ovules and seeds are not enclosed within an ovary.
Elder and viburnum: opposite leaves and small flowers in broad clusters. Often called Adoxaceae in earlier works.
In this atlas: common dogwood, with curved leaf veins and four-petalled flowers.
In this atlas: spindle, with opposite leaves and pink capsules revealing orange seed coverings.
In this atlas: holly, with leathery evergreen leaves and red fruits on female plants.
In this atlas: box, with small opposite leaves and inconspicuous flowers without petals.
A monotypic tropical family of lianas, including the non-carnivorous Dioncophyllum thollonii.
A monotypic Central American family of low shrubs, represented by Guamatela tuerckheimii.
A family of mosses with leafy shoots and conspicuous sporophytes.
The species shown have pea flowers and pods.
In this atlas: heather and bell heather, small woody plants of acid ground with reduced leaves.
What looks like a single flower is a head containing many small florets.
In this atlas: common poppy, with four petals, many stamens and a capsule with pores.
In this atlas: meadow buttercup and lesser celandine, with yellow flowers, many stamens and many carpels.
In this atlas: cowslip, with a basal rosette and tubular flowers with five joined lobes.
A diverse family including foxgloves and plantains here; habit alone does not identify it.
In this atlas: harebell, whose corolla has five fused petals.
In this atlas: sweet violet, with five unequal petals and a spur on the lower petal.
Wild carrot and cow parsley: small flowers in compound umbels and fruits splitting into two mericarps.
In this atlas: stinging nettle, with stinging hairs and small greenish flowers without petals.
In this atlas: dead-nettle and sage, with opposite leaves, usually square stems and two-lipped corollas.
Grasses: narrow sheathing leaves, flowers grouped in spikelets and fruits called caryopses.
Woody plants with alternate, often unequal-based toothed leaves. Elms have small flowers without petals and flat winged fruits.
Mostly woody plants with small four- or five-parted flowers. Buckthorns have fleshy fruits with several stones; leaf arrangement and margins help separate genera.
Flowers usually have four cross-arranged petals and six stamens, four long and two short. Fruits are siliques or silicles, with seeds attached along a persistent partition.
Often opposite, entire leaves with swollen stem nodes. Flowers commonly have five petals, sometimes deeply split. Capsules usually open by teeth or valves.
Flowers usually have five petals; leaves are often palmately divided. The fruit splits into five one-seeded units associated with a long central beak.
Includes dryland plants with varied habits. Balanites has paired leaflets, five-parted flowers and drupes.
Often latex-bearing plants with fused corollas. In Calotropis a five-parted corona surrounds the reproductive column.
Mostly woody plants, often with opposite leaves, inferior ovaries and dry fruits, sometimes winged.
Often herbs with tubular, bilaterally symmetrical flowers and dry capsules; seed and fruit structures vary between genera.
Conifers with scale-like, awl-shaped or flat needle-like leaves. Woody cones have scales often shaped like shields; this family includes the two Californian redwoods.

Nightshade family. Leaves are usually alternate and flowers commonly have a fused, five-lobed corolla with five stamens. Fruits include berries and capsules. Solanum often has conspicuous yellow anthers grouped around the style. A potato tuber is a modified stem, not a fruit.
Family including coffee and bedstraw; leaves often opposite with interpetiolar stipules, flowers with fused corollas.
Citrus and rue family; tissues often bear aromatic glands. Hesperidia characterize citrus, not the entire family.
Often bulbous monocots, usually with six tepals per flower. Onions and garlic belong to subfamily Allioideae.
Often tendril-climbing plants with usually unisexual flowers and inferior ovaries; fruits are frequently pepos.
Tea and camellia family; simple leaves and flowers often bearing numerous stamens.
Pomegranate and loosestrife family; flowers have a floral tube, with varied fruits across genera.
Laurel and avocado family, often aromatic, with small flowers and fleshy fruits.
Aloe relatives: some lineages form succulent rosettes; typically six tepals and six stamens.
Bromeliads: rosette-forming monocots with three sepals, three petals and six stamens; fruits vary.
Banana relatives: large rhizomatous herbs with sheathing leaves, pseudostems and bracted inflorescences.
Ginger relatives: aromatic rhizomatous herbs with asymmetric flowers, usually one fertile stamen.
Palms: monocots with leaves clustered near the growing tip, often compound; flowers generally organized in threes.
Diverse monocots including rhizomatous and bulbous plants; six tepals are common but fruits and vegetative forms differ.
Walnut relatives: woody plants, usually pinnate leaves and separate male and female flowers, often wind-pollinated.
Fig and mulberry relatives: many have latex and reduced flowers aggregated in specialized inflorescences.
Currants and gooseberries: shrubs with palmately lobed leaves; berries develop from an inferior ovary.
Morning-glories and sweet potatoes: usually alternate leaves and funnel-shaped flowers.
Amaranths, quinoa and beet relatives; many have small flowers in dense clusters.
Mostly woody aromatic plants, including star-anise trees of the genus Illicium.
An ancient gymnosperm family represented today by the maidenhair tree, Ginkgo biloba.
Fern family including bracken; fronds bear sori and reproduce by spores, not seeds.
Family including hemp and hops; flowers are small and leaves may be palmately divided.
Tropical family of papaya trees with large lobed leaves and fleshy berries.
Cashew family; often trees or shrubs with small flowers and varied fleshy or dry fruits.
Aroids: tiny flowers sit on a fleshy spadix, often partly enclosed by a showy spathe.
A family of woody climbers and small trees, best known for the kiwifruit genus Actinidia.
A family of mostly aquatic plants with small flowers and whorls of separate achenes.
Succulent family with water-storing leaves, often arranged in rosettes; flowers are commonly five-parted.
Coastal and dryland family that includes sea thrift, with small flowers often grouped in compact heads.
Mostly tropical trees and shrubs; many bear woody capsules, and the family includes the Brazil nut tree.
Carnivorous herbs with glandular leaves that trap small animals; sundews often form basal rosettes.
Ancient conifer family with large trees, broad leathery leaves and cone-bearing reproductive shoots.
Orchid family: flowers have a distinctive lip and column, and many species grow as epiphytes.
Ivy family: often woody plants with alternate leaves and small flowers grouped in umbels or heads; fruits are commonly berries.
Borage family: usually rough-haired plants with alternate leaves and often blue, tubular flowers whose lobes and throat scales help distinguish genera.
Birthwort family: often rhizomatous herbs or climbers; many have distinctive tubular or three-lobed flowers. Some lineages contain toxic aristolochic acids.
Cactus family: succulent stems store water and carry areoles, the specialized structures from which spines, flowers and branches arise; true leaves are commonly reduced or absent.
A family largely of herbs from cool or mountainous habitats; flowers commonly have five parts and fruits are often capsules.
A family of pleurocarpous mosses, often creeping on damp substrates; capsules are borne on setae.
A family of flowering plants including herbs and woody species; flowers are often bilabiate or nearly regular, and fruits commonly capsules.
A small monotypic family of desert woody plants, represented by Koeberlinia; green thorn-tipped shoots bear minute leaves and small dark fruits.
Mostly climbing plants with tendrils, alternate leaves, and distinctive flowers bearing a corona; fruits are usually berries with arillate seeds.
Mostly tropical woody plants; many have simple leathery leaves and regular flowers with numerous stamens. In Lophira the fruit is a nut with enlarged wing-like sepals.
Tropical family of woody or herbaceous plants, often with latex or resins; flowers and berries vary among genera.
Family of small forest monocots, often mycoheterotrophic and lacking chlorophyll.
Small tropical woody family represented by Plocosperma, with tubular flowers and capsules.
Monotypic family of aromatic shrubs from dry regions of Mexico.
Monotypic family of South African fynbos, known for its colorful tubular flowers.
Monotypic family of large East Asian trees with pinnate leaves and winged fruits.
